title: Free radicals: what they are and how they affect health
seoTitle: Free radicals: what they are and how they affect health
subtitle: Learn how they arise, what damage they cause and simple strategies to minimize their effects
excerpt: Free radicals are reactive molecules that damage DNA, proteins and lipids, increasing disease risk; understanding their role aids prevention.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Free radicals are highly reactive molecules that form in the body from natural processes and external factors, and their accumulation triggers cellular damage that impacts long-term health.

What free radicals are

A molecule is considered a free radical when it has an unpaired electron in its outer shell. This loose electron makes the chemical species extremely unstable, causing it to quickly seek another electron to achieve stability. The result is a chain reaction that can spread across various biological structures. These radicals are continuously generated during aerobic metabolism, when oxygen is used to produce energy in the mitochondria. Although production is inevitable, the body has control mechanisms that maintain a balance between the generation and neutralization of these compounds.

How free radicals act on cells

When a free radical hits a macromolecule – such as DNA, proteins or lipids – it can strip electrons from those structures, causing chemical alterations. In DNA, electron removal can generate mutations that accumulate over cell divisions. In proteins, oxidation alters conformation and enzymatic activity, compromising metabolic processes. In membrane lipids, peroxidation reduces fluidity and membrane integrity, facilitating the entry of harmful substances. This collection of damage is called oxidative stress and, when persistent, triggers inflammatory responses and tissue dysfunction.

Everyday sources of free radicals

In addition to internal production, several external agents increase the free-radical load in the body:

  • Ultraviolet radiation from direct sun exposure.
  • Cigarette smoke, which contains thousands of oxidative chemical compounds.
  • Air pollutants, such as fine particles and nitrogen oxides.
  • Processed foods rich in saturated fats, which favor oxidation reactions during digestion.
  • Excessive intensity of aerobic exercise without proper recovery, which temporarily raises radical production in the mitochondria.

These sources are constant in urban daily life, making exposure to free radicals a reality for most people.

Consequences for human health

The buildup of oxidative damage is linked to multiple pathologies. In the aging process, progressive deterioration of support proteins and accumulated DNA mutations favor the appearance of wrinkles and loss of skin elasticity. Regarding cancer, free-radical-induced mutations can activate oncogenes or deactivate tumor-suppressor genes, facilitating neoplasm development. Cardiovascular diseases receive a significant contribution from oxidation of plasma lipids, which promotes the formation of atherosclerotic plaques. In the nervous system, neuronal vulnerability to oxidative stress is associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Thus, an imbalance between production and neutralization of free radicals constitutes a common risk factor for various chronic conditions.

Antioxidant defenses of the body

To counterbalance free radicals, the body possesses a complex antioxidant system. Enzymes such as superoxide dismutase convert the superoxide radical into hydrogen peroxide, which is then broken down by catalase or glutathione peroxidase, producing water and oxygen. These reactions prevent the spread of damage. In addition to enzymes, non-enzymatic molecules play a crucial role: vitamin C donates electrons to neutralize radicals, vitamin E protects lipid membranes, and carotenoids found in fruits and vegetables absorb ultraviolet energy, reducing radical formation. Glutathione, a tripeptide present in all cells, acts as a reducing reservoir, restoring other antioxidant molecules after they act.

Practical strategies to reduce free-radical production

Adopting habits that limit the generation of free radicals and strengthen antioxidant defenses is the most effective way to preserve health. Consuming daily varied portions of fruits, vegetables and legumes provides vitamins, flavonoids and carotenoids that bolster the antioxidant system. Avoiding cigarette use and reducing exposure to highly polluted environments lowers the external radical load. Protecting the skin with appropriate clothing and using sunscreen decreases UV-induced radical formation. Practicing moderate exercise, allowing recovery periods, balances energy production and radical generation. Finally, maintaining regular sleep routines and stress-control techniques supports hormonal regulation, limiting inflammatory processes that can increase oxidative stress.
